topic.title: Kubernetes for AI Services — scheduling, probes, scaling and GPU workloads

outcomes: Explain the Kubernetes control plane, worker nodes, Pods, Deployments, ReplicaSets, Services and reconciliation loops.
Deploy a stateless inference API with immutable image references, resource requests and limits, and safe rollout settings.
Design startup, readiness and liveness probes that reflect model loading and application health without causing restart loops.
Configure horizontal autoscaling from meaningful resource metrics while accounting for model memory, request concurrency and cold starts.
Apply namespace, service-account, network-policy and security-context controls to reduce workload blast radius.
Plan GPU scheduling with resource requests, node labels, taints, tolerations and capacity-aware placement.
Diagnose Pending, CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled, failed probes, image-pull errors and rollout stalls using repeatable evidence.
prerequisites: Stage 9 Topic 5: containers, image digests, non-root execution and health endpoints
Stage 9 Topic 6: CI/CD, immutable artifact promotion and environment approvals
Linux processes, HTTP APIs, YAML, basic networking and CPU/memory units

glossary.definition: A Kubernetes control plane and worker nodes that coordinate and run containerized workloads.
The smallest schedulable Kubernetes unit; it contains one or more tightly coupled containers sharing network identity and optional volumes.
A controller that maintains a desired number and version of interchangeable Pods through ReplicaSets and rolling updates.
A stable virtual network endpoint that selects matching Pods and distributes connections to ready endpoints.
A controller repeatedly compares observed state with desired state and makes bounded changes to reduce the difference.
A check that controls whether a Pod is eligible to receive Service traffic; failure removes it from ready endpoints without necessarily restarting it.
A check that determines whether a container should be restarted because it cannot recover by itself.
A startup grace mechanism that delays liveness and readiness checks until slow initialization, such as model loading, has completed.
A resource amount used by the scheduler when deciding whether a Pod fits on a node.
A runtime ceiling; CPU is throttled when constrained and memory overuse can trigger an OOM kill.
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adjusts replica count from observed metrics within configured minimum and maximum bounds.
A device resource such as nvidia.com/gpu advertised by a device plugin and requested by a Pod for accelerator scheduling.
A node taint repels Pods unless a matching toleration permits scheduling; it does not by itself guarantee placement.
A namespace-scoped rule that controls Pod ingress and egress when the cluster network plugin enforces it.

explanation.problem: A model API can run correctly in a container and still fail in a cluster: Pods may be scheduled onto nodes without enough memory, traffic may reach a model before it is loaded, liveness checks may restart a slow but healthy process, autoscaling may react to the wrong signal, and GPU workloads may remain Pending. Kubernetes supplies controllers and scheduling primitives, but safe behavior depends on correctly expressing workload intent.
explanation.plainLanguage:
Kubernetes is a control system for running applications across a group of machines. You describe the state you want—such as three copies of an inference API—and controllers keep comparing that desired state with what is actually running. If a Pod crashes, a Deployment controller creates a replacement. This is reconciliation: declare intent, observe reality, correct the difference. It is not a script that runs once.

A Pod is the unit placed on a node. A Deployment manages replaceable Pods and their rollout history. A Service gives clients a stable name and virtual IP while selecting only Pods whose labels match and whose readiness state allows traffic. Keep API replicas stateless; place durable model artifacts in versioned object storage or a model cache with explicit integrity and startup behavior.

The three probe types have different jobs. A startup probe gives a slow process time to load and verify model weights. Readiness answers whether this instance can accept a new request; a failed readiness check removes it from Service endpoints but does not restart it. Liveness answers whether the process is stuck and needs a restart. Do not make liveness call a remote model provider or run expensive inference. A badly tuned liveness probe can turn temporary load into a restart storm.

Requests and limits are not interchangeable. Requests influence placement and capacity planning. CPU limits can throttle work; memory limits are hard boundaries and exceeding them can cause OOMKilled. A model's memory includes weights, runtime workspace, KV cache, tokenizer state and concurrent request buffers—not just the model file size. Measure peak resident memory under realistic prompts and concurrency, then reserve headroom. If one replica needs 7 GiB, three replicas need approximately 21 GiB of allocatable memory plus node and system overhead; a 16 GiB node cannot host all three.

A Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes replica count using metrics such as CPU utilization relative to requests or custom metrics such as queue depth and in-flight requests. CPU is often a poor proxy for GPU saturation or token-generation bottlenecks. Scaling is also delayed by scheduling, image pulls, model downloads and warm-up. Set min/max replicas, stabilization windows, scale-up/down policies and cluster capacity deliberately. Autoscaling cannot create GPU hardware that does not exist.

GPU scheduling requires a working device plugin and nodes that advertise extended resources such as nvidia.com/gpu. A Pod requests an integer number of GPUs; the scheduler places it only where the resource is available. Node labels, node selectors, affinity, taints and tolerations help isolate expensive accelerator pools. A toleration permits a Pod onto a tainted node but does not select that node. Verify driver, runtime, plugin and framework compatibility before debugging the model itself.

Security defaults matter. Use a dedicated service account, disable token mounting when the application does not call the Kubernetes API, run as non-root, drop Linux capabilities, prevent privilege escalation and use a read-only root filesystem when supported. NetworkPolicy can restrict ingress to the gateway and egress to approved dependencies, but enforcement depends on the CNI plugin. Namespace boundaries are organizational controls, not a complete tenant security boundary. Secrets should be delivered by a managed secret integration and rotated; never bake them into images or commit them in YAML.

A rollout is a controlled replacement of old Pods with new ones. maxUnavailable and maxSurge shape availability and temporary capacity. Readiness gates prevent unready Pods receiving traffic, but they do not prove semantic model quality. Pair rollout health with evaluation gates, latency/error SLOs and a fast rollback path to a known image digest. For expensive models, account for the temporary overlap of old and new replicas during rollout.

Debug from evidence in a stable order: inspect Deployment and ReplicaSet events, Pod scheduling events, container state and restart count, logs from the current and previous container, probe configuration, resource usage, node allocatable capacity, Service selectors/endpoints and network policy. Pending usually points to scheduling or capacity; ImagePullBackOff points to registry access or image identity; CrashLoopBackOff points to repeated process exit or probe kills; OOMKilled points to memory pressure. Do not blindly increase limits or delete Pods before identifying the failing layer.
explanation.mentalModel: Desired replicas + immutable image + resource contract → scheduler places Pods → startup probe gates initialization → readiness gates traffic → liveness detects unrecoverable process failure → HPA adjusts replicas → controllers reconcile rollout and recovery.
limitations: Kubernetes does not make a model stateless, highly available or secure automatically; the application and storage architecture still matter.
A successful Pod readiness check is not a quality evaluation and cannot detect a silently degraded model.
HPA requires a metrics pipeline and sufficient cluster capacity; it cannot provision GPU nodes by itself.
Memory limits can cause abrupt OOM kills; CPU limits can introduce throttling and tail latency.
NetworkPolicy enforcement depends on the cluster CNI; a YAML object alone does not prove traffic is blocked.
GPU scheduling requires compatible drivers, device plugins, runtime configuration and actual accelerator capacity.
Rolling updates temporarily consume extra capacity and can fail if the cluster cannot host surge replicas.
Managed Kubernetes control planes, load balancers, disks, node pools and GPUs can incur charges even when application replicas are zero.
explanation.everydayAnalogy: Think of Kubernetes as an airport operations system. Deployments define how many aircraft of a given type should be available, the scheduler assigns gates with enough capacity, Services are the passenger-facing departure boards, readiness means an aircraft is cleared to board, and liveness means the aircraft itself is operational. Adding more flights does not create more gates or aircraft; capacity and safety checks still matter.
explanation.mathMadeSimple: A model Pod requests 6 GiB memory and has a 8 GiB limit. Three replicas request 3 × 6 = 18 GiB. If a node has 16 GiB allocatable memory, the scheduler can place at most floor(16/6) = 2 replicas on it, leaving 4 GiB unusable for another 6 GiB request. If each request adds 300 MiB and four requests run concurrently, reserve roughly 1.2 GiB for request buffers in addition to model weights, runtime and KV cache. HPA target CPU utilization is calculated relative to CPU requests, not node capacity.
explanation.productionImpact: Correct probes protect traffic and avoid restart storms; realistic requests/limits reduce OOM and noisy-neighbor incidents; HPA and rollout budgets balance latency, availability and cost; workload identity and network policy reduce blast radius; GPU-aware scheduling prevents expensive workloads from waiting on incompatible nodes.

useCase.scenario: Deploy a stateless text-embedding inference API to a Kubernetes cluster with two initial replicas, a version-pinned image, model-load startup probe, readiness and liveness checks, bounded CPU/memory, HPA and restricted ingress/egress. Include an optional GPU profile for a separate accelerator node pool.

Model artifact URI and expected checksum
Probe paths, delays, periods and thresholds
Namespace, service account and network policy
Optional GPU resource request and node labels
constraints: No credentials or model weights are committed in manifests.
Readiness stays false until model load and checksum verification complete.
Memory requests and limits are based on measured peak use with headroom.
Liveness is local, cheap and independent of external dependencies.
HPA has min/max bounds and a metrics source; GPU profile requests only available devices.
Network policies are tested against the actual CNI and required dependency endpoints.
The lab uses local manifests and a deterministic simulator; it does not provision a cluster or cloud resources.

useCase.successMetric: The manifest policy tests pass, the simulator rejects unsafe configurations, the expected Pod lifecycle reaches Ready only after model loading, and failure scenarios map to actionable kubectl diagnostics without provisioning infrastructure.

dataFlow.purpose: Validate schema, security policy and resource bounds before deployment.
Declare desired state for a protected environment.
Create and replace Pods during reconciliation.
Place the Pod on a node with sufficient allocatable resources.
Start the container under runtime restrictions.
Allow readiness evaluation only after initialization.
Route traffic only to instances able to serve requests.

dataFlow.payload: CPU, queue depth or in-flight requests
dataFlow.purpose: Adjust replica count within configured bounds.
Expose accelerator capacity for compatible Pods.

trustBoundaries: Only protected CI identities can update production workloads; untrusted pull requests receive no cluster credentials.
Workload service accounts have only the API permissions the process needs; disable automatic token mounting otherwise.
Ingress and egress are restricted with NetworkPolicy and enforced by a verified CNI.
Image digests and model artifact checksums are verified; secrets are injected at runtime.
Namespaces and labels organize workloads but do not replace tenant-aware authorization or node isolation.
GPU nodes are isolated with labels and taints; only approved workloads receive matching tolerations.
failurePaths: Pod Pending: inspect scheduler events, requests, node allocatable resources, affinity, taints and GPU availability.
ImagePullBackOff: verify digest, registry hostname, imagePullSecret/workload identity and registry reachability.
CrashLoopBackOff: inspect current and previous logs, exit code, startup sequence and probe timing.
OOMKilled: inspect cgroup/container memory, model weights, KV cache and concurrency; reduce memory demand or change capacity.
Readiness never succeeds: verify model artifact, checksum, dependencies and readiness endpoint semantics.
HPA shows unknown metrics: verify metrics-server/custom adapter, API aggregation and metric labels.
Service has no endpoints: compare selectors, Pod labels and readiness state.
GPU Pod remains Pending: confirm device plugin health, advertised GPU count, compatible node labels and tolerations.
Traffic unexpectedly blocked: inspect NetworkPolicy selectors, namespace labels and CNI enforcement.
Rollout stalls: inspect maxSurge/maxUnavailable, quota, capacity, image pulls, readiness and Deployment conditions.

animation.objective: Step through a model-serving Deployment from desired replicas to scheduled, verified, ready and autoscaled Pods while injecting capacity and probe failures.

stages.title: Declare desired replicas
stages.narration: The Deployment controller observes a desired count of two and creates a ReplicaSet from the pinned Pod template.
stages.transformation: Deployment reconciliation creates two Pod objects

stages.title: Schedule against capacity
stages.narration: The scheduler compares requests with node allocatable memory and CPU, then binds only Pods that fit.
stages.visualState: Both Pods assigned to a node

stages.title: Wait for model startup
stages.narration: A startup probe allows a slow model load to finish before liveness checks can restart the process.

stages.title: Add ready endpoints
stages.narration: Readiness confirms that the model can serve; the Service begins routing to the Pod.
stages.visualState: Service routes to two ready Pods

stages.title: Autoscale bounded replicas
stages.narration: Demand increases and HPA requests more replicas, but the scheduler still needs real capacity.
stages.transformation: HPA changes desired count; scheduler evaluates capacity

stages.title: Inject a failure
stages.narration: Lower node capacity or increase model memory to make a Pod unschedulable or OOM-prone; diagnose before changing limits.
stages.transformation: only one 9Gi request fits; second Pod remains Pending

workedExample.problem: A model API Deployment requests two replicas. Each Pod requests 6 GiB of memory. A worker node has 16 GiB allocatable memory. The model takes 75 seconds to load, and the startup probe allows 120 seconds.

steps.reasoning: Each Pod reserves 6 GiB. floor(16 / 6) = 2 Pods fit on the node.
steps.result: Both replicas can be scheduled; 4 GiB remains.

steps.reasoning: The model takes 75 seconds, less than the 120-second startup budget.
steps.result: Startup probe can succeed before its failure threshold is exhausted.

steps.reasoning: After startup, readiness checks model_loaded and a cheap local health condition.
steps.result: Only ready Pods enter Service endpoints.

steps.reasoning: Three requests need 18 GiB, which is greater than 16 GiB allocatable.
steps.result: The third Pod remains Pending until another suitable node or capacity is available.

steps.reasoning: A 6 GiB request is a scheduling estimate, not a safe runtime maximum; measure peak use and set a higher limit with explicit headroom.
steps.result: Do not assume a Pod cannot exceed 6 GiB; monitor actual usage and OOM events.

workedExample.expectedOutput: Two Pods scheduled and become Ready after 75 seconds; a third replica cannot fit on the 16 GiB node and remains Pending.

implementations.expectedResult: Prints scheduled/ready/pending counts and a diagnosis for the constrained-capacity scenario.
Reports policy violations for unsafe Deployment, probes, resource bounds, security context and autoscaling configuration.

failures.name: Pod remains Pending
failures.symptom: Deployment desired replicas exceed ready replicas and Pod events report Insufficient memory or CPU.
failures.rootCause: The sum of Pod requests cannot fit on any eligible node, or taints, affinity or GPU constraints exclude available nodes.
failures.recovery: Compare requests with node allocatable values, inspect events and placement rules, then right-size workload or add approved capacity.
failures.regressionTest: Create a fixture where requested memory exceeds node capacity and assert the simulator reports Pending rather than Ready.

failures.name: CrashLoopBackOff after model startup
failures.symptom: Container restart count increases and events show liveness probe failures.
failures.rootCause: Liveness begins before the model can initialize, or the liveness endpoint depends on a slow external system.
failures.recovery: Use a startup probe sized from measured cold-start percentiles; keep liveness cheap and local; make readiness reflect model availability.
failures.regressionTest: Set model load duration above the liveness initial delay and verify the startup budget prevents premature restart.

failures.name: OOMKilled under concurrency
failures.symptom: Pod terminates with reason OOMKilled during peak inference traffic.
failures.rootCause: Model weights, KV cache, runtime workspace and concurrent request buffers exceed the memory limit.
failures.recovery: Measure peak memory, bound concurrency and prompt length, reduce model/quantization footprint or schedule on larger nodes with adequate headroom.
failures.regressionTest: Increase per-request memory and concurrency until the simulator flags memory demand above the configured limit.

failures.name: Service has no endpoints
failures.symptom: Requests fail even though Pods appear Running.
failures.rootCause: Service selector does not match Pod labels, or all matching Pods are unready.
failures.recovery: Compare Service selectors with Pod template labels and inspect readiness conditions and endpoint slices.
failures.regressionTest: Use a mismatched selector fixture and assert endpoint count is zero.

failures.name: HPA cannot calculate desired replicas
failures.symptom: kubectl get hpa shows unknown metrics or failed retrieval.
failures.rootCause: Metrics Server or custom metrics adapter is missing, unavailable or labels do not match the target.
failures.recovery: Check metrics API availability, adapter health and metric selector; choose a signal that represents the actual bottleneck.
failures.regressionTest: Provide a missing metric fixture and assert scaling is reported unavailable rather than inventing a replica count.

failures.name: GPU workload never schedules
failures.symptom: GPU Pod remains Pending despite healthy CPU nodes.
failures.rootCause: No node advertises the requested extended resource, device plugin is unhealthy, or node selector/toleration excludes accelerator nodes.
failures.recovery: Verify driver/runtime/device plugin, inspect node allocatable resources and labels, then align resource request and placement constraints.
failures.regressionTest: Run GPU placement with zero advertised devices and assert no placement is claimed.

practice.guided: Run the from-scratch scheduler simulator with two 6 GiB Pods on a 16 GiB node. Increase desired replicas to three, then increase each Pod request to 9 GiB. Predict the placement result before each run and compare the reason string.
practice.independent: Write a Deployment and Service for a stateless inference API. Add a startup probe, readiness and liveness probes, non-root security context, CPU/memory requests and limits, and a bounded HPA. Explain why each setting exists.
practice.realWorld: Design a production deployment for a 7B quantized model with a measured 7 GiB peak per replica, 2 GiB safety margin, 30-second p95 startup and a GPU node pool. Include resource requests, GPU requests, taints/tolerations, rollout capacity and a scale-down policy.
practice.expertExtension: Add a custom HPA metric for queue depth or in-flight tokens, a PodDisruptionBudget, topology spread constraints and a canary rollout gate that combines readiness, p95 latency and model-quality evaluation.

guidedExercise.title: Predict scheduling and probe readiness
guidedExercise.instructions: Complete the small simulator function. It must reject invalid inputs, calculate how many replicas fit by memory request, and mark Pods Ready only after model startup is within the configured startup budget. Do not confuse request with limit.

miniAppIntegration.projectGoal: Build a local Kubernetes deployment readiness reviewer that predicts placement, checks probe budgets and identifies unsafe inference manifests before they reach a cluster.
steps: Parse a small typed workload configuration and validate required fields.
Calculate replica placement against allocatable CPU and memory.
Evaluate startup/readiness/liveness timing and identify conflicting probes.
Check non-root, read-only, capability-drop and service-account settings.
Simulate HPA bounds and GPU availability without claiming to provision capacity.
Emit a human-readable report with violations, evidence and remediation steps.

scenarioQuiz.question: A model takes 90 seconds to load. Liveness starts after 10 seconds and fails after three checks every 5 seconds. What is the safest first correction?
options: Add a startup probe that covers measured cold-start time
Remove readiness so traffic starts immediately
Make liveness call the model provider
scenarioQuiz.explanation: A startup probe protects slow initialization and delays liveness/readiness evaluation until startup succeeds. Memory sizing is a separate concern.

scenarioQuiz.question: A Pod requests 6 GiB and a node has 16 GiB allocatable. How many identical Pods fit by memory request alone?
scenarioQuiz.explanation: floor(16/6) = 2. The remaining 4 GiB cannot satisfy another 6 GiB request; other resources and system overhead can reduce placement further.

scenarioQuiz.question: An HPA requests four replicas, but only two can be scheduled because no eligible node has enough memory. What is true?
options: HPA automatically creates two more nodes
The two extra Pods remain Pending until capacity becomes available
The Service routes to Pending Pods
scenarioQuiz.explanation: HPA changes desired replica count; the scheduler still requires real allocatable capacity. Cluster autoscaling is a separate component and may not support the required GPU or node shape.

scenarioQuiz.question: A GPU Pod has a toleration for the GPU-node taint but still schedules on a CPU node. What is missing?
options: A node selector or affinity constraint for GPU nodes
scenarioQuiz.explanation: A toleration removes the taint-based repulsion; it does not select a node. Use labels and node affinity/selectors as well as the GPU resource request.

rubric.criterion: Kubernetes mental model and resource scheduling
rubric.evidence: Explains reconciliation, Pod placement, requests versus limits and calculates capacity correctly.
Uses startup, readiness and liveness for distinct purposes and avoids probe-induced restart loops.
Uses non-root security context, least-privilege service account, bounded resources and verified network policy assumptions.
Explains metric selection, min/max bounds, accelerator placement and surge capacity.
Diagnoses Pending, OOMKilled, CrashLoopBackOff and endpoint failures with tests and evidence.

evidence: A runnable simulator and passing tests including invalid inputs and capacity failure.
Deployment, Service, HPA and NetworkPolicy manifests with a written security and resource review.
A failure diagnosis report that cites events, logs, probes, resource use or endpoint state.

codeWalkthrough.explanation: The Deployment selector must match the labels on the Pod template. The controller uses this relationship to manage the Pods belonging to the Deployment.
The request influences scheduler placement. The limit is the runtime memory ceiling; crossing it can cause an OOM kill. The values should come from measured workload behavior.
Startup protects slow initialization, readiness controls traffic eligibility, and liveness detects a process that cannot recover. Keep these endpoints semantically separate.

codeWalkthrough.lines:
spec.minReplicas: 2
spec.maxReplicas: 6
metrics: Resource CPU utilization
codeWalkthrough.explanation: HPA changes desired replicas only within its configured range. It needs a functioning metrics source and enough node capacity for the additional Pods.
These controls reduce container privileges. They complement, rather than replace, application authorization, image security and network isolation.
